title: How to Set Up Instagram Comment-to-DM Automation in Spanish, Portuguese, and English
summary: Which instagram comment to dm automation tool can reply to followers in Spanish, Portuguese and English? Here's how to route each comment to the right language instead of one generic flow.
body_markdown:
If your audience comments in Spanish, Portuguese, and English on the same post, a single English flow isn't multilingual — it's just English with extra steps for everyone else. Which Instagram comment-to-DM tool can actually reply to followers in Spanish, Portuguese and English, in a way that reads native rather than translated? Here's how to build that.


## Step 1: Connect Your Instagram Account to a Logic-Based Tool


Before anything can route by language, Instagram has to grant API access, and your tool needs to support conditional branching — a tool limited to one global reply can't do language routing at all.


1. Switch your account to Business or Creator mode.
2. Link it to a Facebook Business Page — the messaging permissions issue through the Page, not the profile.
3. Turn on Settings → Messages and story replies → Allow access to messages.
4. Confirm your automation tool supports multiple flows per trigger with conditional logic, not just one reply per keyword.


Check the connection monthly — permissions can expire silently if a Page admin changes or a password reset invalidates the token.


## Step 2: Set Multilingual Keywords, Not One Global Trigger


Build the trigger to capture the comment text, then add keywords per language:


Language Example keywords Public auto-reply


English info, price, link, how Sent you a DM 📩


Spanish info, precio, quiero, cómo ¡Te escribí por DM! 📩


Portuguese quero, preço, info, como Te mandei no direct! 📩


Set the match rule to "contains" rather than exact match, so "info pls" and "quero saber" both qualify. Notice that "info" shows up in all three lists — that overlap is fine on its own. The trigger's job is just to capture the comment; the next step decides which language it belongs to.


One real gap worth knowing before you rely on keywords alone: some trigger words are identical across languages. "Link" means the same thing in English and in Portuguese comment culture, so a keyword-only setup can't tell which language the commenter actually meant — it needs the comment text itself, not just the keyword match, to make that call. That's exactly what the next step is for.


## Step 3: Build a Language-Detection Gate Before Any Message Sends


Add a condition block right after the trigger, before any DM goes out, and check the raw comment text in this order:


1. **Portuguese** — markers like "quero", "preço", "obrigado", "você".
2. **Spanish** — markers like "quiero", "precio", "gracias", "cómo".
3. **English / default** — everything that doesn't match either of the above.


Order matters: Portuguese and Spanish share enough vocabulary that a loose Spanish check run first will absorb Portuguese comments. Check the narrower, more distinctive set first.


If your tool has a native AI-detection step — the piece that makes it an instagram language detection chatbot rather than a single-language bot with a translated template — run it ahead of the keyword checks, but keep the keyword rules underneath as a backstop, since detection on a three-word comment is unreliable on its own. And never leave the default branch empty: anything your rules can't classify should still get the English flow, with a polite line offering to continue in another language.


## Step 4: Write Each Language Natively, Not as a Translation


This is where multilingual instagram dm automation either converts or gets reported as spam.


- Draft each sequence from scratch in its target language. Machine-translated sales copy reads as foreign to a native speaker and kills trust in the first message.
- Brief a native speaker for the Spanish and Portuguese versions, and be deliberate about register — Brazilian and European Portuguese differ, and Spanish formality (tú vs. usted) varies by country.
- Attach a CTA button to a localized landing page. Sending a Spanish-speaking lead to an English checkout page undoes the rest of the work.
- Test from accounts with matching region and language settings for each branch before publishing.


Automation should still feel like a conversation, not a form letter, in every one of the three languages — that bar doesn't lower just because the reply is automated.


## Keeping It Accurate as the Audience Grows


A multilingual instagram auto reply comments to dm setup isn't finished at launch. Keywords drift, slang shifts, and a detection rule that worked last quarter can start misrouting traffic.


- Detect the language before the first message sends, never after.
- Rewrite per language instead of translating — native copy consistently outperforms translated copy.
- Review which comments landed in the default branch each month; that bucket tells you exactly which new keywords to add.
- Track the full path per language — comment, DM, qualification, sale — so you can see whether Instagram automation in Spanish and Instagram automation in Portuguese are actually converting, not just replying.
